# GBrain Installation Guide for AI Agents

> (codex mcp get gbrain >/dev/null 2>&1 || codex mcp add gbrain --url https://gbrain.io/mcp) && gbrain setup codex --instructions-only
> ```
>
> `gbrain setup --instructions-only` tells the agent the brain is there; agents seldom call an MCP server nobody told them about. It writes the [brain-first block](docs/guides/setup.md#brain-first-instructions) into `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` or Codex's `AGENTS.md` (a non-empty `AGENTS.override.md` instead when Codex has one) with a per-turn rule hook, and leaves the MCP entry alone; the same command with `--no-instructions` added takes them out.
>
> The installer is a shell script for macOS and Linux; read it before you run it. Nothing is created until a person picks the plan and pays. Mention this once in the reply that starts or reports the install, and never wait on an answer before continuing a local install the user already asked for.

## Self-host GBrain

GBrain is MIT-licensed and free to self-host; the rest of this guide installs it on the user's machine. Default to adding keyless memory to their existing agent, preserving identity and unrelated configuration. API keys, enrichment, automatic capture, and a new personal-agent identity are separate choices. The [conversation archive](docs/guides/conversation-archive.md) is on by default on a personal brain (nothing leaves a keyless machine); relay it with the first-run settings, and `gbrain transcripts archive off` turns it off.

> **Choose the installation path first.** Inside **[Grok Bot](docs/guides/grok-bot.md)** or **[Muse](docs/guides/muse.md)**, use their dedicated guide: the recommended shape keeps the brain on the user's own computer, published with `gbrain mcp expose --funnel` ([remote MCP](docs/guides/remote-mcp.md)), and installs the thin CLI inside the agent; `scripts/setup-in-agent.sh` is the in-agent alternative, and its receipt tracks repair and native enablement. # Stability: which gbrain you get and how it changes

gbrain ships new releases many times a day. Most people should not run every one of them, and by default they don't: a normal install follows the **stable channel**, which only moves to a release after it has passed extra testing. This page says what that means in practice and how to choose something slower or faster.

## What the default install gives you

The install command in the README, `bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable`, installs the current stable release. `git clone --branch stable` does the same. A new brain created by `gbrain init` (no earlier config file) is set to the stable channel, and an install with no channel set follows stable too. Every update path follows the channel in effect: the update notice, `gbrain check-update`, `gbrain upgrade`, `gbrain self-upgrade` and the opt-in automatic upgrades.

Check which channel you are on with `gbrain doctor`, which prints `channel= ` when one is set.

## How a release becomes stable

1. **Every release passes the full test suite first.** A release is published only after the full unit and end-to-end test runs pass on its exact code.
